6º de Primaria · Inglés

Countable and uncountable nouns

Ficha para imprimir
123456
1

Pregunta de arranquePiensa 30 segundos antes de seguir

Puedes decir «three apples» (tres manzanas), pero ¿puedes decir «three waters» o «three breads»? ¿Por qué?

Escribe o di en voz alta tu respuesta. Después .

Porque water y bread son nombres incontables: no se cuentan uno a uno. Para contarlos usamos un recipiente o una porción: «three bottles of water», «two pieces of bread». En cambio, apple es contable: one apple, two apples.

2

Aprende14 apartados

Para empezar: The great pancake disaster

It was Mum's birthday, and my sister Nora and I wanted to make her pancakes for breakfast. We found a recipe online, but we didn't read it carefully.

The recipe said: «200 grams of flour, two eggs, 300 millilitres of milk, a pinch of salt and a little butter.» We didn't have any scales, so we used cups. I put in three cups of flour. That was too much. Nora added a lot of milk to fix it. That was too much milk! Then she added some sugar, but it wasn't sugar: it was salt!

The mixture was like soup. We poured a few spoonfuls into the frying pan, and the kitchen filled with smoke. The smoke alarm started beeping and Mum and Dad ran downstairs in their pyjamas.

Mum looked at the black pancakes, the flour on the floor and our faces covered in white powder. Then she started to laugh.

«It's the best birthday present ever,» she said. «Now, let's make them together. And this time, let's measure everything!»

1. Countable or uncountable?

Countable nouns are things we can count one by one: an apple, two apples; a chair, three chairs; a friend, ten friends. They have a singular and a plural form.

Uncountable nouns are things we can't count one by one, like liquids, materials and some foods: water, milk, juice, rice, sugar, bread, cheese, money, music, homework. They have no plural: we never say «rices» or «musics». En castellano: pasa algo parecido con «arroz» o «leche»; no decimos «tres arroces».

2. Countable: singular and plural

With singular countable nouns we use a or an: a banana, a sandwich, an egg, an orange (an before a vowel sound). We can't say just «I want banana»: we need a.

Plurals usually add -s: apples, carrots. After -s, -sh, -ch, -x and some -o words add -es: glasses, sandwiches, potatoes, tomatoes. Consonant + y → -ies: strawberry → strawberries, cherry → cherries. Irregular: child → children, person → people, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, mouse → mice.

3. Always plural: a pair of

Some nouns in English are always plural. They are usually things that have two parts that are the same:

  • Clothes: trousers, jeans, shorts, pyjamas, tights, leggings.
  • Tools and objects: scissors, glasses, sunglasses, binoculars, headphones, pliers.

These nouns take a plural verb: «My jeans are blue.» «Where are my glasses?» «These scissors don't cut well.» We never say «a trouser» or «a scissor».

To count them, we use a pair of:

  • «I bought a pair of trousers.» (unos pantalones)
  • «She has three pairs of jeans.»
  • «Can I borrow a pair of scissors?»

Notice: with a pair of, the verb is singular: «This pair of shoes is too small.»

En castellano también decimos «unos pantalones» o «unas tijeras» en plural para una sola cosa, ¡así que no es tan raro! Pero cuidado con otras palabras: en inglés shoes, socks y gloves sí tienen singular: «a shoe», «a sock», «a glove».

4. Uncountable nouns

Uncountable nouns use the verb in singular: «The water is cold», «Rice is good for you», «My homework is difficult». We don't use a or an with them: not «a bread», but «some bread».

Common uncountable nouns: food (bread, rice, pasta, cheese, meat, butter, sugar, salt), drinks (water, milk, juice, tea), and also money, time, music, information, homework, furniture, weather. En castellano: ojo con homework o furniture (muebles), que en inglés no tienen plural.

5. Countable or uncountable? It depends!

Some nouns can be countable or uncountable, but the meaning changes a little:

  • chicken: «There's a chicken in the farm» (the animal, countable) / «I'd like some chicken» (the meat, uncountable).
  • coffee: «I don't drink coffee» (the drink in general) / «Two coffees, please» (two cups of coffee, in a café).
  • paper: «I need some paper» (the material) / «Dad reads a paper every day» (a newspaper).
  • glass: «The window is made of glass» (the material) / «a glass of water» (the object).
  • hair: «She has long hair» (all the hair) / «There's a hair in my soup!» (one single hair).
  • time: «I don't have time» / «I've been to London three times» (occasions).
  • cake: «Would you like some cake?» (a piece) / «Mum made two cakes» (whole cakes).

Tip: ask yourself if you are talking about the material, the substance or the idea in general (uncountable) or about separate units that you can count (countable).

6. Some and any

We use some in affirmative sentences, with plural countable nouns and with uncountable nouns: «There are some eggs», «I'd like some water».

We use any in negatives and questions: «There aren't any eggs», «Is there any milk?». Exception: offers and requests use some in questions: «Would you like some cake?». En castellano: some es «algo de / algunos»; any en negativa es «nada de / ningún».

Vídeo: Some y any en inglés · Inglés para niños con Mr Pea (YouTube) · 424 mil visualizaciones

7. How many? How much?

To ask about quantity: How many…? with plural countable nouns and How much…? with uncountable nouns. «How many apples do we need?» – «Six». «How much sugar do we need?» – «A little» / «200 grams».

In the same way: many (muchos) with countable and much (mucho) with uncountable in negatives and questions: «There aren't many people», «I haven't got much time». A lot of goes with both: «a lot of friends», «a lot of water».

Vídeo: Much vs many · Inglés para niños con Mr Pea (YouTube) · 357 mil visualizaciones

8. A few and a little

For a small quantity we say a few with countable nouns and a little with uncountable nouns: «I've got a few friends in Madrid», «Can I have a little milk in my tea?».

From most to least: a lot of → some → a few / a little → not any / no. En castellano: a few es «unos pocos» y a little es «un poco de». Fíjate en que el inglés distingue si se puede contar o no, y el español casi nunca.

9. Containers and pieces

To count uncountable things we use containers (recipientes) or portions: a bottle of water, a glass of milk, a cup of tea, a carton of juice, a packet of rice, a jar of honey, a can of lemonade.

Portions: a piece of cake, a slice of bread / pizza / cheese, a bar of chocolate, a kilo of meat, a loaf of bread (una barra). The container is countable: «two bottles of water», «three slices of pizza».

10. Recipe English

Recipes are full of countable and uncountable nouns, quantities and imperatives. Here's a simple recipe for pancakes:

Ingredients (for 8 pancakes): 200 grams of flour · 2 eggs · 300 millilitres of milk · a pinch of salt · a tablespoon of sugar · a little butter.

Method:

  • First, put the flour, the sugar and the salt in a big bowl.
  • Then, add the eggs and a little milk and mix well.
  • Next, add the rest of the milk slowly and whisk until there are no lumps.
  • Heat a little butter in a frying pan. Ask an adult to help you!
  • Pour a ladle of the mixture into the pan. Cook for about one minute on each side.
  • Finally, serve with fruit, honey or chocolate.

Useful quantities: a pinch of (una pizca), a spoonful / teaspoon / tablespoon of (una cucharada), a slice of (una rebanada), a cup of, grams and millilitres. Useful verbs: add, mix, pour, whisk, heat, cook, cut, serve.

Vídeo: How to Make Pancakes at Home | Easy Pancake Recipe · Hands Touch (YouTube) · 29,6 millones de visualizaciones

11. Reading: a shopping list

Read the dialogue in the kitchen: «Mum: We're going to make pancakes. How many eggs have we got? Dani: There are a few, only two. Mum: We need three. And how much milk is there? Dani: There's a little, half a carton. Mum: OK, let's write a list: six eggs, a carton of milk and a bag of flour. Is there any sugar? Dani: Yes, there's a lot of sugar. And can we buy some strawberries? Mum: Of course!»

12. Let's practise: at the market

Role-play in pairs: one is the shop assistant and the other is the customer. «Good morning! Can I help you?» – «Yes, please. I'd like a kilo of tomatoes and some cheese.» – «How much cheese?» – «Two slices, please.» – «Anything else?» – «Have you got any bananas?» – «Sorry, there aren't any.»

Consejo: antes de preguntar, piensa: ¿se puede contar? Si sí, How many; si no, How much.

13. Don't waste food!

Every year, huge amounts of food end up in the bin. According to the United Nations, about one fifth of the food available to people in shops, restaurants and homes is wasted, and most of it is thrown away at home. At the same time, hundreds of millions of people in the world don't have enough food to eat.

Wasting food also wastes the water, the energy and the land we used to produce it, and rotting food in rubbish dumps produces gases that make climate change worse.

What can we do? Here are some ideas:

  • Make a shopping list and buy only what you need.
  • Don't put too much food on your plate. You can always have a bit more later.
  • Check the fridge: eat the food that is getting old first.
  • Use leftovers: stale bread can become breadcrumbs or French toast, and old bananas make delicious banana cake.
  • Freeze food that you can't eat in time.

Do a survey at home: how much food do you throw away in a week? How many pieces of fruit? Then try to reduce it. Small changes in every home can really make a big difference for our planet.

Vídeo: Desperdicio de alimentos: El costo oculto de los alimentos que desechamos | ClimateScience #9 · ClimateScience - Solve Climate Change (YouTube) · 501 mil visualizaciones

14. Food from around the world

Many foods we eat every day came from other parts of the world. Read and notice the countable and uncountable nouns:

  • Potatoes, tomatoes, maize (corn) and chocolate came from the Americas. Before the 16th century, there wasn't any chocolate in Europe, and Italian cooks didn't use tomatoes!
  • Rice came originally from Asia, and so did oranges and tea.
  • Coffee came from Africa, from the region of Ethiopia.
  • Pasta, bread and cheese have been popular around the Mediterranean for thousands of years.

Notice: rice, tea, coffee, pasta, bread, cheese and chocolate are uncountable. We say «some rice», «a lot of pasta», «a piece of cheese», «a bar of chocolate». But potatoes, tomatoes and oranges are countable: «three potatoes», «a few oranges».

Think about your favourite meal. Where did its ingredients come from? Make a world map with the ingredients of your favourite dish!

Spanish sailors and explorers played an important part in this story. In the 16th century, ships brought potatoes, tomatoes and cocoa beans from the Americas to Spain, and from there they travelled to the rest of Europe. At first, many Europeans didn't trust potatoes and tomatoes: some people thought they were strange or even dangerous! It took a long time for them to become popular. Today, it's difficult to imagine Spanish food without them: think of tortilla de patatas, gazpacho or chocolate con churros.

Ejemplos resueltos

Ejemplo 1. Countable or uncountable: rice, egg, juice, carrot.

  1. egg y carrot se cuentan: an egg, two carrots.
  2. rice y juice no se cuentan.

Resultado: Countable: egg, carrot. Uncountable: rice, juice.

Ejemplo 2. Complete: «How ___ bread do we need?»

  1. bread es incontable.
  2. Incontable → How much.

Resultado: How much bread do we need?

Ejemplo 3. Complete with some or any: «There isn't ___ cheese, but there are ___ eggs.»

  1. Negativa → any.
  2. Afirmativa → some.

Resultado: There isn't any cheese, but there are some eggs.

Ejemplo 4. Correct: «I need a new trouser.»

  1. Trousers is always plural.
  2. To count it, use a pair of.

Resultado: I need a new pair of trousers.

Ejemplo 5. Countable or uncountable? «I'd like ___ chicken, please.» (the meat)

  1. The meat is a substance.
  2. Uncountable: some.

Resultado: I'd like some chicken, please.

Errores típicos

  • Poner plural a un incontable: «breads», «homeworks» → «bread», «homework».
  • Usar a con incontables: «a water» → «some water» o «a glass of water».
  • Confundir How many y How much: «How many money?» → «How much money?».
  • Usar some en negativas: «There aren't some eggs» → «There aren't any eggs».
  • Olvidar los plurales irregulares: «childs», «peoples» → «children», «people».
  • Decir «a scissor» o «a trouser»: se usa a pair of.
  • Decir «an information» o «two breads»: son incontables.

Ejercicios (24)

Hazlos en tu cuaderno y después abre la solución.

Nivel básico

  1. Write the plural: potato, strawberry, box, foot.

    Ver solución
    potatoes, strawberries, boxes, feet.

  2. Countable or uncountable? milk, chair, money, sandwich.

    Ver solución
    Uncountable: milk, money. Countable: chair, sandwich.

  3. Complete with a or an: ___ orange, ___ banana, ___ egg.

    Ver solución
    an orange, a banana, an egg.

  4. Write three nouns that are always plural.

    Ver solución
    trousers, scissors, glasses.

  5. Complete: «Where ___ my glasses?» (is / are)

    Ver solución
    are.

  6. What does «a pinch of salt» mean?

    Ver solución
    Una pizca de sal.

  7. Name two foods that came from the Americas.

    Ver solución
    Potatoes and tomatoes (also chocolate, maize).

  8. Complete: «I bought two ___ of jeans.»

    Ver solución
    pairs.

Nivel medio

  1. Complete with some or any: «Have you got ___ brothers?»

    Ver solución
    any.

  2. Complete: «How ___ people were there?»

    Ver solución
    many.

  3. Complete: «Can I have a ___ of pizza?»

    Ver solución
    slice (o piece).

  4. Complete with a few or a little: «I've got ___ friends in Bilbao.»

    Ver solución
    a few.

  5. Correct: «I need an information.»

    Ver solución
    I need some information.

  6. Explain the difference: «a paper» / «paper».

    Ver solución
    A paper is a newspaper; paper is the material.

  7. Choose: «There's (a hair / hair) in my soup!»

    Ver solución
    a hair.

  8. Write the first three steps of the pancake recipe with first, then, next.

    Ver solución
    First, put the flour, sugar and salt in a bowl. Then, add the eggs and a little milk. Next, add the rest of the milk.

  9. Give three tips to waste less food.

    Ver solución
    Make a shopping list, take small portions, use leftovers (freeze food).

  10. What mistakes did the children make in the reading?

    Ver solución
    Too much flour, too much milk, salt instead of sugar.

Nivel avanzado

  1. Translate: «¿Cuánta agua hay?»

    Ver solución
    How much water is there?

  2. Write your breakfast with quantities.

    Ver solución
    Model answer: I have a glass of milk, two biscuits and a piece of fruit.

  3. Write a recipe for your favourite sandwich with quantities and imperatives.

    Ver solución
    Open answer.

  4. Do a food waste survey at home for three days and write five sentences with how much / how many.

    Ver solución
    Open answer.

  5. Explain «two coffees» and «coffee» with examples.

    Ver solución
    Two coffees = two cups (in a café); coffee = the drink in general.

  6. Make a world map of the ingredients of a Spanish dish (for example, tortilla de patatas).

    Ver solución
    Open answer. Potatoes from the Americas, eggs, olive oil from the Mediterranean, onion.

¿Has nombrado estas ideas?
★

Situación de aprendizajeZero waste cookbook

La clase crea un recetario en inglés con recetas para aprovechar las sobras y reducir el desperdicio de comida.

Pasos

  1. Pedid en casa recetas tradicionales que aprovechen sobras (torrijas, croquetas, migas…).
  2. Escribid cada receta en inglés con ingredientes, cantidades e imperativos.
  3. Añadid un dato sobre el origen de un ingrediente y un consejo contra el desperdicio.
  4. Maquetad el recetario y compartidlo con las familias.

Producto final: Un recetario bilingüe «Zero waste cookbook».

Cómo se valora

  • Uses countable and uncountable nouns correctly.
  • Uses quantities and imperatives in recipes.
  • Gives advice about food waste.
  • Writes clearly and accurately.

Tarjetas de repasoToca la tarjeta para darle la vuelta

Según cómo respondas, la tarjeta vuelve mañana, en 3, en 7 o en 21 días.

Para familias

  • Escribid juntos en inglés la lista de la compra de la semana con cantidades: «a carton of milk, six eggs».
  • Al cocinar una receta sencilla, preguntad «How much…?» y «How many…?» por cada ingrediente.
  • Repasad juntos las tarjetas del paso 6 dos minutos al día durante una semana.

Para profesores

Saberes: Alimentación y compras; nombres contables e incontables, cuantificadores y partitivos (Lengua Extranjera) (RD 157/2022, tercer ciclo de Primaria).

  • Mercado simulado en clase con precios y tarjetas de productos.
  • Receta en inglés con lista de ingredientes y cantidades.
  • Clasificar tarjetas de comida en dos cajas: countable / uncountable.

Qué vas a aprender

  • Tell the difference between countable and uncountable nouns
  • Use a / an, some and any correctly
  • Ask about quantity with How many…? and How much…?
  • Use containers to count uncountable things: a bottle of, a piece of
  • Use nouns that are always plural with a pair of
  • Recognise nouns that can be countable or uncountable
  • Read and write a recipe with quantities
  • Talk about food waste with how much, how many and a lot of

Palabras clave

countable · uncountable · a / an · some · any · How many…? · How much…? · a lot of · a bottle of · a piece of

Tiempo

80 minutos hoy + 2 minutos en cada repaso
